query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An integrated in situ method combining high-temperature XRD with real‐time thermogravimetric monitoring under a controlled oxidizing atmosphere will simultaneously capture both oxidation kinetics (e.g., weight gain and oxide scale growth) and transient phase transformations more accurately than separate ex situ measurements.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-temperature alloy (e.g., a high-entropy alloy or superalloy) in its as-cast or initially stabilized phase state with no pre-formed oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Implement an integrated experimental setup that couples high-temperature XRD (ideally enhanced by synchrotron radiation for improved time resolution and sensitivity) with real-time TGA, all performed under a controlled oxidizing environment.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 750–1100 °C) under a well-controlled oxidizing atmosphere to mimic service conditions, ensuring that both oxidation kinetics and phase evolution occur concurrently.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamic formation and evolution of oxide scales on the alloy surface, which coincides with underlying phase transformations within the bulk material.
generation.mechanism: By recording XRD patterns in real time alongside continuous TGA data, the integrated method correlates the kinetics of weight gain (from oxidation) with the emergence or transformation of crystalline phases. This simultaneous monitoring overcomes the limitations of ex situ methods that miss transient phase behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated in situ method will reveal synchronous changes in weight (indicative of oxidation rate) and phase transitions (identified via XRD), providing a more detailed and temporally correlated understanding of oxidation kinetics and phase stability than when using separate TGA and post-mortem XRD measurements.
generation.baseline: Using conventional ex situ thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) for oxidation kinetics combined with post-mortem XRD for phase analysis, which only provides discontinuous snapshots of the evolving system.
generation.boundary: The method’s advantages are expected only under high-temperature conditions with precisely controlled oxidizing atmospheres; complexities may arise at lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments where the coupling between oxidation and phase transformation is less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the ultimate time resolution achievable for very rapid phase transitions, and whether synchrotron-enhanced detection uniformly improves sensitivity for all types of phase changes. Additionally, the integrated approach may face challenges in decoupling overlapping signals in highly complex systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled high-temperature oxidation experiment on an alloy sample under a fixed oxidizing atmosphere using both the integrated in situ (XRD coupled with TGA) method and conventional ex situ methods (separate TGA and post-mortem XRD). Compare the temporal correlation between weight gain and phase evolution across both techniques.
measurements: Continuous weight gain curves from TGA
Real-time XRD pattern acquisition to monitor phase changes
Post-experiment oxide scale thickness analysis via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated in situ technique does not provide significantly enhanced temporal correlation between oxidation kinetics and phase evolution (i.e., both datasets are not more synchronously coupled than in the separate ex situ approach), or if it fails to capture transient phase changes that are otherwise observable, then the hypothesis is falsified.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Earlier research relied on conventional, ex situ techniques—such as thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) for oxidation kinetics and separate post-mortem X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification—to study high-temperature oxidation and phase stability. This approach proved inadequate because it could not capture the transient, real‐time evolution of phases during oxidation. Over time, researchers began implementing in situ methods (e.g., high-temperature XRD, and in situ TEM) to monitor oxidation processes and phase transformations concurrently, although even these techniques sometimes fall short when it comes to simultaneously correlating weight gain with phase evolution under exactly controlled oxidizing environments.
decision.unsolved: The key unsolved challenge is the lack of an integrated experimental method that can capture real‐time oxidation kinetics (such as weight gain and oxide scale growth) concurrently with the detailed evolution of transient phases under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
decision.lever: Integrate in situ high-temperature XRD with real-time thermogravimetric monitoring under controlled oxidizing conditions (potentially using synchrotron radiation for enhanced time resolution and sensitivity)
decision.why: This lever directly addresses the limitations identified in the trend by combining the strengths of both kinetic (TGA) and phase identification (XRD) measurements in a single experimental setup, enabling simultaneous observation of oxidation kinetics and phase transformations in real time as indicated by recent advances and the needs outlined in the research question.
